en: Commentary on the Verses of the Universal Gate Chapter,
composed by the Śramaṇa Zunshe of the Tianzhu Monastery during the Song Dynasty.
△ The second set of verses was translated by Jñānagupta during the Daye era of Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty, following the passing of the Great Master Zhiyi.

Since we are now entering the main body of the great treatise, the commentary lacks an explanation of the *Linggan zhuan* (Account of Miraculous Responses) regarding the celestial and human speech. Master Nanshan said: "Master Kumārajīva was an eighth-stage Bodhisattva;

in his translation of the *Lotus Sūtra*, he omitted the *Guan-yin chong-song* (Repetition Verses on Avalokiteśvara). Since it involves matters of karmic retribution from the unseen realm, one can believe that such a text exists.

Now, I shall support the two preceding sections of questions and answers by providing a brief explanation following the text, though it is difficult to exhaustively clarify the underlying principles. Let the lecturer simply...
To ensure that the general outline of the preceding passage is not lost, why must one strive for novelty? This hymn consists of twenty-six lines, divided into two parts:
first, a single verse that poses two questions together; second, twenty-five verses that provide answers to these two questions.
Within the initial question, one line praises his virtue, while three lines pose the actual inquiry.
"The World-Honored One is endowed with wondrous marks.
Within this single phrase, the name and the essence are combined to praise the name of the World-Honored One.

Thus, by briefly citing his honorific title, one understands that the preceding nine [phrases] together constitute the essential praise for the Most Honored One among the three periods of time. "Endowed" refers to the substance; "marks" refers to the wondrousness.

"Endowed with the marvelous" (*suvibhakta*) is a term of praise. "Endowed" (*suvibhakta*) refers to the fulfillment of the thirty-two marks. Furthermore, "marvelous" (*su-*) means "excellent" (*bhadra*);

it signifies that his physical form is made excellent by being adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). Furthermore, this praises both the name and the reality of the Dharma-body. "Name" refers to the marvelous name;

"characteristics" refers to the marvelous characteristics. As the preceding text states: "He is endowed with the thirty-two marks, and by the eighty... [the eighty secondary characteristics complete the description].

The ten kinds of excellent marks that adorn the Dharma-body are precisely what is intended here. One who possesses these marks and excellences (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) is one who possesses the two types of adornment;
because such a person is able to answer my question, they are raised up and praised.
I now ask again: for what causes and conditions is that Son of the Buddha named Avalokiteśvara?

In this initial sentence of the formal inquiry, two questions are combined; the phrase "asking again" refers to repeating the inquiries made regarding the two preceding sections—how could one say otherwise?
The subsequent two sentences inquire specifically about Avalokiteśvara, desiring that the Buddha first answer the first chapter.
This is because it is further corroborated by what follows nearby; one may also ask all three phrases together.

Since the first chapter already presents the self-invited response and subsequent answer, and since there is the subtle benefit of the true body (*dharmakāya*), how could there not be the manifest arrival in response to conditions?
Therefore, within the explanation of "allowing," both instances are permitted—namely, hearing the name and seeing the body.
△ In the second response, three points are established: the first two verses provide a general response to the two chapters; the next nineteen verses provide a detailed response to the two chapters;
and the final four verses exhort one to uphold the name and offer worship as a general response.
Within the general response, the first verse provides the direct answer, and the subsequent verse relies on the fundamental contemplation of compassion.
The Honored One, endowed with wondrous marks, answered the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati in verse: "Listen to the practices of Avalokiteśvara, who appropriately responds to all regions.
His great vows are as deep as the ocean; throughout inconceivable eons, he has served many thousands of billions of Buddhas and made vast, pure aspirations."

"Listen to the practice of Avalokiteśvara"—this is the general answer to the preceding chapter on how Avalokiteśvara derives its name from the conditions of both object and wisdom, and how he skillfully responds to all regions;
this is the general answer to the subsequent section on the universal gate manifestations. One should apply this general meaning to interpret [the following].
Next, one verse traces back to the original contemplation and compassionate vows to reveal the present wisdom and abandonment (jñāna-prahāṇa) and the tenfold benefits.
This is based on the four truths of the Distinct and Complete [vehicles], which are immeasurable and unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*). From these, one gives rise to vows and practices;
because the objects of these vows are profound and vast, the great vows are like the ocean. "Great" (*hong*) means "vast. Throughout successive kalpas, the manifestation of time is long and distant;

within each and every kalpa, one serves many thousands of billions of Buddhas. Furthermore, in the presence of each and every Buddha, one again formulates distinct vows, such as the forty [great vows].

Because each of the eight vows individually encompasses the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they are further described as "great" (*mahā*). Regarding the passage of kalpas, there is the vertical dimension;
regarding the service rendered, there is the horizontal dimension. Within each vertical instance there is the horizontal, and within each horizontal instance there is the time traversed.

This shall be explained in detail (as follows). Taking this general summary of the original vows, one applies them below to answer each specific difficulty, as well as the Universal Gate chapter that follows.
The details may be understood through extensive explanation.
△ Second, the specific response is further divided into two parts; the first verse is a dual affirmation that explains the two chapters:
"I shall briefly explain for you that hearing the name and seeing the body and mind are not in vain; they can extinguish all suffering within the realms of existence."
The mention of "hearing the name" is the permission granted in the preceding chapter; the mention of "seeing the body" is the permission granted in the subsequent chapter.

Regarding the present instruction to listen, the statement "briefly explained" constitutes the specific response (*vyākaraṇa*), while the "general response" contains manifold implications, such that the text is concise while the meaning is extensive.

The specific response sets forth the details, clarifying the seven calamities and so forth from the perspective of the realms of beings and their karmic retribution; the Universal Gate section, meanwhile, focuses primarily on the thirty [types of practitioners].
The equality of the three bodies is expressed through extensive text but concise meaning; taking this concise meaning now, it is clear that "hearing" is permitted as a distinct response.
"Hearing the name" refers to the names of the object and wisdom of Avalokiteśvara. The preceding text explained the meaning of the three types of wisdom by way of four kinds of hearing;
both aspects of "contemplation" can be understood accordingly. "Seeing the body" refers to the manifestation of the Universal Gate, revealing the three karmas of the responsive body.

The phrase "the mental recollection is not in vain" clarifies that there should be benefit in two stages. Since this mental recollection belongs to the faculty of mind (*manas*), it does not mention body or speech;
this is because it subsumes the discourse of the two chapters according to the two types of capacities—latent and manifest—for the sake of linguistic convenience. Why is this so?

In the first chapter, regarding the manifest capacity, whether it be body or speech, both must be governed by the mind; therefore, the mind is able to subsume them all. Thus, the previous explanation of "holding the name" states: [text continues].

The mouth recites and upholds, while the mind maintains and sustains; though it is not "upheld by the mouth," discernment and observation (*vitarka-vicāra*) are vocal activities that generally belong to the category of vocal karma.
For example, in the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*, holding the name with a single mind without distraction does not preclude the vocal activity involved;
as the subsequent passages all say, "recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara," this case is analogous.
The explanation of the latter section on the "dark mechanism" (míngjī) can be understood by taking the "concentration of the mind" as the basis;
thus, it is clear that what is not empty is such that even if one recites the name without manifesting any visible proof, the hidden benefit is not in vain.
△ The twenty-eighth verse provides the direct response, which is divided into two parts: first, thirteen verses praising the initial chapter; second, five [verses].
Following the verses, the first chapter consists of two parts: first, twelve verses clarifying the responsive manifestations of the karmic faculty of speech;
second, one line briefly summarizing the responsive manifestations of the two faculties of body and mind. The seven difficulties mentioned in the preceding text represent the six great elements;
furthermore, even when many other difficulties are cited, they likewise represent these. Now, in this verse, the two mountains of falling and the wild beasts and snakes are added.
Scorpions—these four are all comprised within the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*). Poisonous drugs are comprised within the seeds of human, insect, and ghost consciousness.

Dust and physical matter are comprised within the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*). Rain and hail are comprised within the water element (*ap-dhātu*). Furthermore, when combined with the six calamities caused by *rākṣasa* ghosts, they form twelve difficulties;
the first verse concerns the difficulty of fire.
Even if one should give rise to a harmful intent and push another into a great pit of fire, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, that fiery pit shall turn into a pond.
The preceding text is explained through three categories: first, the application of the text to provide evidence for the practice and realization;

second, within that realization, the initial extensive section concerns ten instances of encountering suffering where the invocation of the name establishes the capacity to evoke a response; third, this is followed by a discussion of the two types of "abiding dharma"—the distinct and the perfect.
The gates, compassion, and vows clarify the ten realms mentioned previously; their perfect benefit is now briefly annotated with a single explanation.

The remainder may be inferred from what precedes, so they are not recounted in full detail. The lecturer should fully demonstrate their meaning so that the contemplation of the principles is not obstructed, thereby benefiting those who come after.
Regarding the "great pit of fire," the text above simply says "great fire"; this [term] is added here.
Because the pit was vast and even deeper, it was intended to manifest that the power of the Sage is such that no fire, however great or small, can cause him difficulty; how much less so a large pit?

Even if the *kalpa*-fire were to rise from the hells up to the First Dhyāna Heaven, filling such a great pit with glowing flames, the Bodhisattva could still either blow it out, inhale it with his mouth, or shield it with his hand to extinguish it.
Those who do not burn may instead find cool ponds.
△ Next, one verse concerns the peril of water:
"Whether drifting upon the vast ocean or facing the terrors of dragons, fish, and various spirits, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, the waves cannot submerge them."
If one reaches a shallow place above, one can avoid calamity; yet even a shallow place becomes fearsome if dragons and ghosts are present.
Thus, when encountering conditions for death, the multiple instances mentioned in the preceding text further manifest the Sage’s spiritual response.
△ Next, one verse concerns the peril of falling from Mount Sumeru:
"Whether on the peak of Mount Sumeru one is pushed by others and falls, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one dwells like the sun in the void."
Just as the sun abiding in the sky reveals its inconceivable power, so too is this [the Buddha's power] merely a conventional designation; who could possibly reach it?

Furthermore, even if one were pushed away and such a thing occurred, there is nothing the Sage would not do for them. King Māndhātṛ was able to ascend to Mount Sumeru, yet because of his craving for the imperial throne, he descended back to the human realm.
If one can invoke his name, there is certainly a principle by which one will be saved.
△ Fourth, the verse on the difficulty of falling from Mount Kāñcana:
"If one is pursued by an evil person and falls onto Mount Vajra, by the power of calling upon Avalokiteśvara, not even a single hair can be harmed."
△ 51. One verse on the peril of hostile bandits:

If one encounters hostile bandits surrounding them and each brandishing blades to inflict harm, by the power of mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara, they shall all immediately give rise to a compassionate heart.
△ 61. One verse on the peril of kings:
Or if one encounters the suffering of royal punishment and faces execution at the point of death, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, the blade shall instantly break into pieces.
(67) One verse on the hardship of shackles and fetters:

Or if one is imprisoned and bound with shackles and fetters, and the hands and feet are constrained by cangues and manacles, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one shall be released and attain liberation.
△ Verse 81: The Difficulty of Poisons and Curses.
When various poisons and curses intended to harm one’s body are directed at a person who recollects the power of Avalokiteśvara, they return to the sender themselves.

Although his great compassion and impartial love ought to eliminate [harm] equally for all, the reason they return to the sender is that it is the very recipient of the name-recitation who is being harmed.
One must certainly save those who can harm one; when there is no opportunity [for them to harm], one subdues the evil mind within oneself, for this is not caused by a sage.

Furthermore, if a poisonous spirit possesses someone, it must either kill the other person or inevitably harm oneself. Question: If one subdues the evil mind within oneself, why is it that toward an enemy or thief one only causes [the mind] to give rise to loving-kindness?
Answer: Because the act of harming by the thief is manifest, merely causing [the mind] to give rise to loving-kindness is sufficient to reveal [the truth].
The efficacy of sacred power, poisons, and secret plots to cause harm has been proven; yet there are also cases where the perpetrators harm themselves.

For example, an old monk of Donglin Temple was struck by bandits, but the bandits instead stabbed themselves with their swords, the blades entering at the heart and exiting from the back, while the rest of the gang fled in all directions.

Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that poisons do not necessarily always rebound upon the user, it is explained through the dual application of *śamatha* (calming) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). If...

If both [the practitioner and the obstructing spirit] possess the necessary conditions (*mārga*), then this may be so; however, if the one who would cause harm lacks the conditions for either the hidden or manifest response, then even such a refutation is applied in vain.
△ Ninth: One verse on the peril of *rākṣasa* demons.
If one encounters evil rākṣasas, venomous nāgas, various ghosts, and the like, when they call upon the power of Avalokiteśvara, none dare to cause harm.

Furthermore, before the venomous nāgas there are fish-dragons and ghosts; these are mentioned repeatedly because nāgas and ghosts range over both water and land, whereas those previously mentioned were restricted to the water alone (as detailed in the passage on the four kinds of nāgas, etc.).
△ Verse 11: The Peril of Fierce Beasts.
If one is surrounded by fierce beasts with fearsome sharp teeth and claws, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one shall flee swiftly to the boundless directions.
△ Verse 12: The Peril of Snakes and Scorpions.
The venomous breath of vipers, snakes, and scorpons blazes like smoke and fire; yet by the power of Avalokiteśvara, they turn back upon hearing his voice.
△ Twelve: One verse on the calamity of rain and hail.
When clouds and thunder roll, lightning flashes, hail falls, and great rain pours down, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, these are dispersed and dissolved at that very moment.

For those who wish to benefit practitioners of contemplation, one should skillfully explain this through the gateways of evil karma and afflictions as being like snakes and tigers, thereby aligning it with the correct principle;
if one follows the *Qing Guanyin Shu* (Commentary on the Invocation of Avalokiteśvara), one should clarify the power and function of dispersal and subduing according to its threefold meaning.

That is to say, by way of phenomena (*vastu*), practice (*caryā*), and principle (*nyāya*), one should understand this by correlating it with the resultant retribution (*vipāka*), afflictions (*kleśa*), and the dharma-gates (*dharmaparyāya*) therein;
thus concludes the section on the responsive manifestation of verbal karma (*vākkarma*).
△ The second verse summarizes the two types of responsive manifestations—bodily and mental:
"When sentient beings are beset by calamities and oppressed by immeasurable suffering, the wondrous power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom can rescue the world from its pain."
The three poisons raging violently so that the mind lacks self-mastery is called "distress. Four classes of beings dwell together, each describing their own suffering:
the pigeon says that lust is the greatest suffering; the snake says that hatred is the greatest suffering (and so forth). Regarding the woman’s suffering of childlessness, it is as explained above.

Alternatively, one may divide this into two phrases, correlating them with the mental and the physical, which can be understood through careful analysis. If one practices contemplation to understand this, [the meaning will become clear].
The tenth section concerns those who are afflicted by the three poisons and establishes the gates of the *anuloma* (concordant) and *pratiloma* (inverse) methods beyond the realms;
this should be explained by applying the meaning of the preceding text to resolve the significance of the three poisons.

Regarding the statement that "the bodily karma lacks progeny and lacks the cultivation of causes for male or female, even up to the lack of male or female in the Perfect and Sudden teachings," one should seek its resolution in the preceding text. If both mental recitation and physical prostration constitute the karmic capacity, [then...]
Because it eradicates the roots of the three poisons, fulfills the two adornments, and forever uproots the sufferings of the ten realms and the three lands of the mundane world,

it is said that "the wondrous power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom can rescue the world from suffering. One should also further clarify the compassion of the fundamental contemplation of the Distinct and Perfect [teachings] (and so forth).
△ Second, five verses specifically answer the "Universal Gateway Manifestation. While the text here is concise compared to the preceding specific sections, it still functions as a general summary.
This section is further divided into three parts: first, two verses praise the universal manifestation; second, two verses praise the fundamental contemplation;
third, one verse concludes with the noble ones' three types of action. Within the first part, there are again two sub-sections: the first verse directly praises the universal manifestation.
The second verse specifically enumerates the three types of *dharmadhātu* for those to be converted.

Possessing the power of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*) and extensively cultivating the skillful means of wisdom (*jñānopāya*), there is no land throughout the worlds of the ten directions in which he does not manifest his body.
Through various evil destinies—birth as hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals, and the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death—he causes them all to be gradually extinguished.
In the preceding passage, the bodies of the sages were listed as extending from the Palace of the Vajra Devas down to the realm of hell;
here, the inferior is cited to illustrate the superior, thereby establishing their mutual inclusion. Each body is explained according to four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) as previously stated.
Furthermore, while the preceding passage took the three lands (*tri-bhūmi*) as the objects of response, these ten directions should now be explained in terms of the three lands (and so forth).

△ Next, the two verses on the fundamental contemplation are further divided into two parts: the first verse concerns practice and vows, while the second verse concerns the accomplishment of contemplation and its universal benefit.
Within the first part, there are three sections: two lines distinguish the contemplation, one line expresses the vow of compassion, and one line exhorts toward taking refuge.

The Contemplation of Reality, the Contemplation of Purity, the Contemplation of Vast Wisdom, the Contemplation of Compassion, and the Contemplation of Loving-kindness—may one always aspire to and gaze upon them.

The Contemplation of Reality realizes emptiness and achieves all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*); the Contemplation of Purity emerges from the provisional realm and, being untainted by existence or non-existence, achieves the Knowledge of the Paths (*mārgajñatā*);
the Vast Wisdom is the contemplation of the Middle Way that pervades all phenomena, which is called "Vast and Supreme" as it transcends the two extremes.
The "extremes" refer to the Middle Way; its essence is wisdom. Because one contemplates this essence, it is called the "contemplation of wisdom.

Question: Why is wisdom named the "middle essence"? Answer: This follows the intent of this sutra. This sutra takes the Dharma-body as its essence—characterized by quiescence and illumination—and takes response and resonance as its primary tenet.
Thus, such a statement can be made: the three types of wisdom are actually realized within a single mind.

Regarding the statement that "compassion, discernment, and so forth cannot be [regarded as] identical or different," this is because their vows are collectively termed "discernment" (*vipaśyanā*) since they arise by taking the truths as objects;
it is just as the ten dharmas of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are collectively named "discernment.
△ Next, the verse distinguishes the benefits, which is further divided into two parts.
The sun of wisdom with its stainless, pure light breaks through all darkness; it can subdue the winds and fires of calamity and shines universally upon the world.
The first two lines clarify the light of wisdom, while the subsequent two lines clarify how the light of compassion destroys darkness and illuminates the world (and so forth).
△ 31. One verse concludes by manifesting the three types of noble activity:

With the thunderous roar of the precepts whose essence is compassion, and the wondrous great cloud of a benevolent mind, he pours down the nectar rain of the Dharma to extinguish the flames of affliction.

The "thunder of precepts" corresponds to bodily action (*kāyakarman*); the "clouds of loving-kindness" correspond to mental action (*manaskarman*); and the "pouring rain" corresponds to verbal action (*vākkarman*).

The precepts restrain the seven branches of conduct, with bodily action being the primary focus; because the purity of these precepts can uproot the suffering of the three evil realms, they are called the "essence of compassion.

The manifestation of supernatural powers through the wheel of the body startles and moves the multitude, resembling the shaking of thunder. The internal affection and mindfulness are named "loving-kindness," which universally covers all beings.

Like clouds that respond without premeditation yet meet with circumstances without fail, it is further called "wondrous mental karma. The wheel of speech expounds the Dharma of the true mark as a rain of ambrosia;
the three types of grass and two types of trees equally receive its nourishment, and the feverish afflictions of the three delusions are thereby cooled.
Its extensive explanation of the three types of non-conditioned [knowledge] and the three types of non-guarding is as described in the preceding section.

First, regarding the traces [of the Buddha], each instance of preaching the Dharma must clearly distinguish the *via media* (Zhong), *Sudden* (Duan), and *Perfect* (Yuan) teachings; only when one understands the dharma-gates in which the Bodhisattvas abide can their practical application be realized.
This concludes the section on the "Universal Gate" (*Pumen*).
△ Third, four verses exhorting upholding and making offerings, which are further divided into two parts. The first two lines and one phrase exhort upholding.
Section Two: One Verse in Three Lines Exhorting to Offerings. This section has two parts. First, one line reiterates the previous karmic response of speech as an exhortation:
"In the midst of disputes before the courts, or within the terrors of military ranks, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, all enemies will completely retreat and scatter."
Regarding the preceding oral karma, it is listed first because citing one encompasses two; thus, official litigation and military conflict are specifically mentioned.
Difficulties from water and fire are rare, while matters involving ghosts and tigers are few; one encounters disputes only when fortune declines.

Disputes are common in the world, rooted in wealth, beauty, fields, and houses—things encountered daily. Therefore, encouraging the observance [of precepts] is essential. As for weapons and imprisonment, they exist in the hidden realm.
Furthermore, encountering military arrays, royal levies, and forced labor is not of one's own choosing;

moreover, when contending by force, one faces the peril of being struck down by sharp blades and weapons, or the hardship of death through long-term imprisonment and legal records. When one’s wealth is plundered by bandits, it is not as dire as being caught in an army;
this, too, is an essential point for exhortation.

△ Next, one line and one phrase correctly provide the exhortation, which is further divided into two parts: the first three phrases employ provisional and ultimate teachings for comparative evaluation, and the final two phrases conclude with the exhortation.
"The Sound of Wondrous Voice, the Sound of Avalokiteśvara, the Brahma-Sound, and the Tide-Sound surpass all worldly sounds."

First, taking up the Bodhisattva’s actual realization and actual benefit as the standard for comparison, [the text] states that they surpass the provisional vehicles of the nine realms because their compassion and wisdom are superior.

Thus it says, "surpassing the sounds of the world. This refers to a single phenomenon—the sound-dust (*śabdadhātu*)—which, when viewed with the Buddha-eye of actual wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*), is the wondrous sound of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*);
yet when viewed with the Dharma-eye of provisional wisdom (*upāyajñāna*), it is the worldly sound of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*). This is the actual realization.
Furthermore, cultivating compassion based on the Middle Way is called the "Brahma-voice"; this compassion can provide opportunities for beings and is thus called the "Ocean-tide Voice.

This is a true benefit, as it is like never failing to accord with the proper measure. Compared to the two types of compassion—the compassion for sentient beings and the compassion for phenomena within the nine realms—which merely involve mental attention and respond to objects, how could they possibly be comparable?
Therefore, it is said that it "surpasses them"; the comparison and evaluation are clear.
△ Second, the two lines conclude with an exhortation:
"Therefore, you must constantly maintain mindfulness in every thought-moment and not give rise to doubt.

The initial exhortation to constant mindfulness consists of two practices: that of phenomena (*dharma*) and that of principle (*tattva*). (As explained at length... If these practices of phenomena and principle are perfected, one will personally realize Bodhi.
The phrase "Because of the two bodies of the person and the dharma" further halts doubt and offers encouragement.
Next, the first line of three phrases encourages making offerings; the first phrase is a praise:
"Avalokiteśvara, the pure and holy one."
Because the Bodhisattva’s three karmas are pure, arising from right livelihood, he is called a "Pure Sage" (*śuci-ārya*);

this means he is worthy of receiving offerings. Right livelihood is the Dharma of the Sages; because people receive this Dharma, they are called sages. Thus, it is said: "Avalokiteśvara, the Pure Sage.
Next, his specific virtues are enumerated individually to serve as an exhortation.
△ Regarding the two lines following "in suffering and distress," these verses praise the virtue of bestowing fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*).
It means being able to act as a refuge for those facing the calamities of suffering and death;
"suffering and death" refers to the state of fear and calamity, while "acting as a refuge" refers to the power of fearlessness. It is like a young child relying [on its parents].

"Having parents as protectors, what more need one fear?"—this refers to the provisional and ultimate bodies manifested before one, whom he designates as "parents" to protect the children of the Three Vehicles and deliver them from the calamities of the two deaths.
△ The four lines beginning with "Possessing all... cite the field of merit to offer exhortation.
Possessing all merits, he gazes upon sentient beings with eyes of compassion; his ocean of accumulated blessings is immeasurable, and for this reason, he should be honored with prostration.
"Possessing all merits" refers to the Bodhisattva’s *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body). "Gazing upon sentient beings with eyes of compassion" refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
"Ocean of accumulated blessings" is a general praise of these two fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), which are as exalted as mountains; "accumulation" (*caya*) signifies their vast gathering.
That which is profound, vast, and boundless is called the ocean; this also praises the Dharmakāya as the basis for the two fields [of merit].
"Prostrate" is an exhortation to make offerings through the three karmas. Because the physical manifestation is evident, it is specifically mentioned;

yet, since one must necessarily possess all three karmas, the preceding text omits the necklaces (hārāḥ), whereas here they are mentioned alternately. Furthermore, this exhortation applies universally to all.
All may obtain the merit of making offerings with necklaces of a hundred pieces of gold; who could discern this? Furthermore, that which is honored by the noble is surely not something trivial.
For one who contemplates the mind: if the activity of the body is diligent, it increases merit and virtue, which is the offering to the Nirmāṇakāya (Response Body);

if the activity of speech and mouth is active, it explains Prajñā, which is the offering to the Saṃbhogakāya (Enjoyment Body); if the activity of the mind is diligent, it accords with principle, which is the offering to the Dharmakāya (Dharma Body).
The commentary on the verse regarding the *dharmakāya* (etc. is concluded.
The commentary on the *Geya* (repeated verses) of the "Universal Gate" Chapter is finished.
The commentary by the Venerable Ciyun of the Song Dynasty, circulated separately, has been appended to the main body of the canon; thus, the teachings of the South [are complete].
This garden [of teachings] had not been transmitted for nearly two hundred years. In the Jia-wu year of the Zhizhi era (1294), I entered the capital for the sake of the Dharma;
at Hongfa Temple in the city of Yanjing, I obtained this text. Returning to the east, I found it to be indeed authentic.

Fearing that I might keep it secret, I have therefore carved it into printing blocks to benefit future students of the Great Virtue. Written by the bhikṣu Xingcheng, resident monk of Xingyuan, in the fifth month of summer in the Ren-yin year (1302).
Respectfully Submitted as a Preface.
